title: Why Do Bees Matter?
paragraphs: Although bees are usually associated with honey, their greatest contribution is pollination. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar and pollen, they transfer pollen grains between plants, enabling fertilisation and, in turn, the production of fruit and seeds.

The domesticated honeybee is only a small part of the story. Scientists have described roughly 20,000 bee species, and wild bees such as bumblebees and solitary bees are often more efficient pollinators of certain crops. Butterflies, flies, birds and bats contribute as well.

International assessments estimate that around 75 per cent of the leading global food crops benefit to some degree from animal pollination, including many fruits, nuts, vegetables, coffee and cocoa. While staple grains such as wheat and rice are pollinated by the wind, the foods that provide much of our vitamins and variety depend heavily on pollinators.

In many regions, pollinator populations are declining. Researchers point to a combination of pressures: habitat loss, intensive agriculture, certain pesticides, parasites and diseases, and a changing climate that can disrupt the timing between flowering and insect activity. Protecting wildflower habitats and reducing pesticide use are among the most effective responses.
